description_full: PulteGroup, Inc., through its subsidiaries, engages in the homebuilding business in the United States. The company is involved in the acquisition and development of land primarily for residential purposes, as well as construction of housing; and sale of single-family detached homes; and attached homes, such as townhomes, condominiums, and duplexes under the Centex, Pulte Homes, Del Webb, DiVosta Homes, and John Wieland Homes and Neighborhoods brands. It also engages in the mortgage banking, title, and insurance agency operations. PulteGroup, Inc. was founded in 1950 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.
ceo_bio: Mr. Ryan R. Marshall | President, CEO & Director | Age 50 | Compensation: $6.3M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 6K people. Revenue per employee of $2.7M ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, with revenue growing 9%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $269K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $8K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: PulteGroup, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $23.4B market cap on $17.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

The business throws off $1.7B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.84× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.27 vs 5y 0.97), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $199.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 62% in the 2020 crash, 36% in the 2022 bear market and 59% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $114 (margin of safety -12%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $94.24 to $141 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 13.6 vs 18.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.5% (above the risk-free rate).
The 17 covering analysts target $132 on average, 4% above the price.
The price implies 0.1% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp more than the model expects.
prof: It converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.9B (8% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.2% over 3 years, 9.4% over 5 years and 11.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Free cash flow has compounded 0.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 0.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 2.2% on average.
Analysts expect 1.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $18.8M sold).
It returns 5.9% a year to shareholders (5.1% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 6.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, raising it 6.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,506 employees, each generates about $2.7M of revenue, 7.0x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 9.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $269K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.3M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
